planting.note: Start seed indoors over a very lean mineral cactus mix in warm conditions, as this slow-growing, monotypic genus can take the better part of a decade from seed to first bloom.

directions: Leuchtenbergia principis is the sole species in its genus and unmistakable among cacti for its long, blue-green, triangular tubercles that radiate outward like the leaves of a small agave, each tipped with papery, twisted spines that curl as the plant ages. Unlike true agaves, the tubercle tips are true cactus areoles, and large lemon-yellow flowers up to 3 inches across open from the newest growth in late spring, often with a light sweet fragrance. It differs from superficially similar Ariocarpus and Ferocactus in its elongated, non-overlapping tubercles rather than a compressed rosette or ribbed body. Give it full sun, a fast-draining mineral substrate, and minimal water, especially in winter, since the swollen taproot rots quickly in damp soil.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Start seed indoors over a gritty mineral mix in consistent warmth, then grow on for several years before hardening off; unlike lowland columnar cacti, this high-altitude Andean species tolerates brief, dry cold snaps once established but still needs winter protection from prolonged freezes and wet soil.

directions: Oreocereus celsianus forms clustering columns clothed in long, silvery-white wool that insulates the stem from intense high-altitude sun and temperature swings in its native Andean grasslands of Peru, Bolivia, and Argentina, with stout amber to reddish-brown spines emerging through the hair. Funnel-shaped magenta-pink flowers open low on the stem in summer, distinguishing it from the similarly woolly Cephalocereus senilis, whose flowers are white and nocturnal and whose native range is Mexican rather than Andean. Grow in full sun with a very mineral, fast-draining substrate; the wool sheds water and traps grit, so avoid overhead misting and let the soil dry fully between waterings. Its high-elevation origin gives it more tolerance of cool, dry conditions than most columnar cacti, though prolonged freezing or winter wet is still fatal.

planting.note: Start seed indoors in warm conditions over a fast-draining mineral mix, and give young plants strong overhead light from the outset, since low light dulls the powdery blue coloration that makes this species so sought after in landscapes and large containers.

directions: Pilosocereus pachycladus is a fast-growing, tree-forming Brazilian columnar cactus prized for the intense powder-blue, waxy bloom that coats its ribbed stems, an effect strongest on new growth in full sun and easily rubbed off by handling. Older stems develop a dense, woolly patch of white or golden hair near the areoles from which nocturnal, white, bell-shaped flowers open in summer, followed by round reddish-purple fruit. It is distinguished from the similarly blue Myrtillocactus geometrizans by its solitary, non-branching-from-base columns and true hairy areoles rather than smooth ribs. Site in full sun with excellent drainage and let soil dry between waterings; container specimens can be moved indoors near a bright window over winter in cold climates.

planting.note: Start seed indoors over a lean mineral mix in warm conditions; plants stay globular for years before slowly elongating into a short column, and being the sole species in its genus, seed-grown stock should always be sourced from reputable specialty nurseries rather than wild collection.

directions: Denmoza rhodacantha is a monotypic Argentine cactus that begins as a dense, ribbed globe bristling with long, flexible reddish spines that give the genus its 'fire barrel' nickname, only gradually becoming columnar after ten or more years. Tubular orange-red flowers roughly 2 inches long open near the crown in a loose ring during late spring and summer, distinguishing it from true barrel cacti (Ferocactus and Echinocactus) that flower in a full crown ring rather than a partial arc. It tolerates cooler nights and light frost better than many South American globular cacti thanks to its high-elevation Andean foothill origin, but still requires a gritty, fast-draining substrate and a dry winter rest to avoid rot. Grow in full sun for the best spine color.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Start seed indoors over a very lean, slightly acidic mineral mix, since this Brazilian species grows on quartzite outcrops and resents the alkaline, calcium-rich mixes used for most cacti; it is also notoriously sensitive to overwatering and stagnant humidity, so err toward underwatering while establishing.

directions: Uebelmannia pectinifera is a slow-growing Brazilian cactus whose columnar, ribbed body is coated in a waxy, near-black to deep purple-brown epidermis, with neat rows of comb-like (pectinate) white spines lying flat against each rib, a texture and color combination found in few other cacti. Small yellow flowers cluster in a woolly patch at the growing tip once plants reach several inches tall, usually after many years of cultivation. It differs from the superficially similar Copiapoa in its true pectinate spine arrangement and quartzite-habitat origin in Minas Gerais rather than coastal Chile. Because it grows naturally in humid, high-rainfall mountains rather than true desert, it tolerates slightly more moisture and humidity than typical globular cacti but still demands sharp drainage and bright light, with afternoon shade appreciated in hot climates to prevent scorch.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Start seed indoors over a mineral cactus mix in warm conditions; this species flowers and offsets readily within a few years, making it one of the more forgiving Coryphantha for beginning collectors.

directions: Coryphantha elephantidens forms a solitary or slowly clustering blue-green globe covered in unusually large, blunt, five-sided tubercles that give the species its common name, each tipped with a small areole bearing short, stiff spines rather than the long central spines typical of the genus. Its standout feature is a crown of very large flowers, often 3 to 4 inches across in shades of magenta-pink to pale rose, disproportionately big for the plant's compact size and rivaling many Echinocereus in flower display. It is distinguished from Mammillaria, which it superficially resembles, by producing flowers and fruit from the current season's areoles near the crown rather than from the axils between older tubercles. Grow in full sun to light shade with a mineral, fast-draining mix and a dry winter rest to encourage heavy spring bloom.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Start seed indoors in warm, humid conditions over a mineral mix, and keep humidity moderate through the seedling stage; this Cuban species is more compact and quicker to form its flowering cephalium than most other Melocactus, often within 3 to 5 years.

directions: Melocactus matanzanus is one of the smallest species in its genus, forming a compact blue-green to gray-green ribbed globe only 3 to 4 inches across before switching to reproductive growth and producing a cephalium, a bristly, woolly cap of reddish-pink hair and spines at the crown that the stem itself never grows beyond again. Small pink flowers emerge from the cephalium in summer followed by slender, bright pink-red fruits that push up above the wool, a display unique among globular cacti and the source of the genus's 'Turk's cap' nickname. Because it hails from coastal Cuba rather than an arid desert, it appreciates more warmth and humidity than most cacti and is notably less cold-tolerant, needing protection whenever temperatures drop much below 50°F. Grow in full sun with a mineral, fast-draining mix and consistent warmth for the cephalium to develop properly.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
